picked.title: DexPort: A Hand-Held Skill Interface for Dexterous Hand Data Collection
picked.summary: Collecting high-quality demonstrations remains a central bottleneck for learning dexterous manipulation. Teleoperation records executable robot actions, but it requires a complete robot setup and places the burden of coordinating many finger joints on the operator. Human demonstrations are easier to collect, but their motions must be estimated and retargeted to the robot, and they do not directly provide robot actions. In this paper, we introduce DexPort, a portable data-collection interface for high-DoF robot hands. It uses the same hand hardware for collection and deployment, avoiding a hand embodiment gap, and records both commanded joint targets and measured joint states. Our key observation is that a small set of skills can support a wide range of dexterous tasks. During collection, the operator moves the hand-held interface to specify the robot wrist motion and selects or adjusts skills that coordinate the finger motion. This removes the need to control each joint independently while retaining behaviors such as precise grasping and in-hand manipulation. We collect demonstrations across several real-world tasks and in unstructured environments without a robot arm. We then use behavior cloning to train visuomotor policies directly on the recorded wrist motions and hand commands, without skill labels. We evaluate across 4 tasks: pick-and-place with diverse objects, screwing with in-hand tool use, drawer stowage which requires simultaneous grasp and pulling, and a bimanual scanning task. We collect over 2,500 demonstrations with our portable device, in both laboratory and in-the-wild settings. Across our tasks, we see an improvement from 11% to 64% when using recorded robot commands instead of states, and an improvement from 36% to 78% for task success when using in-the-wild data.

picked.title: DiscoDemo: Discovering Efficient and Diverse Robot Demonstrations for Imitation Learning
picked.summary: Behavior cloning for robotic manipulation is highly sensitive to the coverage of its training data, yet collecting diverse successful demonstrations remains costly. We study reinforcement learning (RL) not as a deployable controller, but as a data generator for downstream visuomotor imitation learning. Our key premise is that multiple successful solution modes cover a broader range of successful trajectories than repeatedly collecting a single narrow solution. We introduce DiscoDemo, which trains a privileged latent-conditioned RL generator with a parallel reverse curriculum and a success-gated diversity objective to discover diverse solutions while preserving task success. The trained generator produces multiple successful closed-loop behaviors, which are safety-filtered and exported as a static dataset for downstream imitation learning. Across four manipulation tasks, DiscoDemo produces broader successful-state coverage and improves downstream visuomotor policies in both simulation and the real world. Averaged across tasks, downstream success increases to 62% from 40% for the strongest baseline in simulation, and to 78% from 39% on the real robot, respectively. These results suggest that successful solution diversity improves imitation learning for a pretrained flow-matching VLA and remains complementary to corrective data collection. Project page: https://davian-robotics.github.io/DiscoDemo

picked.title: Coupling Execution Horizon and Sampling Depth in Flow-Matching VLA Policies
picked.summary: Flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate expressive continuous trajectories for robotic manipulation, yet balancing real-time responsiveness with execution stability remains a persistent challenge. Standard deployment workflows typically treat numerical solver depth and execution horizon as decoupled choices. The horizon amortizes inference latency, while solver depth is kept high to preserve integration fidelity. In this paper, we reveal a fundamental compute-execution coupling in flow-matching VLAs governed by a systematic sign reversal. While coarse numerical integration degrades precision under rapid replanning, it markedly improves task performance under extended open-loop commitment. Geometrically, numerical truncation contracts lateral action dispersion around an invariant trajectory centroid, serving as an implicit regularizer that suppresses compounding open-loop drift. Across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world Franka manipulation on representative VLA backbones including $π_0$, $π_{0.5}$, and GR00T, exploiting this joint coupling consistently achieves superior task success while drastically lowering inference latency, entirely training-free and without architectural modifications. These findings establish numerical sampling depth as an operational variance regulator, shifting its role from a static precision budget to an active deployment knob in robot learning. Project page: https://jiabingyang01.github.io/Horizon-Depth-VLA/

picked.title: Geometry-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Close-Fitting Wearable Insertion
picked.summary: Robot-assisted dressing is particularly challenging due to narrow openings and articulated body parts. Even small errors in the relative pose between the body part and garment opening can cause snagging, missed insertion, or incomplete dressing. To address these challenges, we formulate dressing as a geometry-aware insertion problem that represents task-relevant spatial relationships between the body part and object opening, rather than relying on the full deformable-object state. Based on this formulation, we propose a Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework combining a staged curriculum, which progressively guides the policy from coarse alignment to insertion and final placement, with a finger-wise insertion soft gate that provides continuous feedback on individual finger insertion progress and helps suppress premature insertion. We evaluate the framework on rigid and deformable bracelet dressing tasks through component ablations, systematic variations in the initial hand pose, and closed-loop execution of the learned policies on a real robotic system. On the post-training deformable evaluation, the full method reaches 84.7 +- 1.2% success. The insertion gate accounts for the largest gain, and adding the curriculum on top of that gate reaches the top score. On a mannequin hand the same full policy succeeds on 15/20 real-robot trials.

picked.title: Isaac Lab Interactive browser demos
picked.summary: Prebuilt Newton WebAssembly simulations, their browser viewer, and exporter source for Isaac Lab documentation. The documentation stages one reviewed, commit-named archive and verifies its SHA-256. This release is the permanent bundle container; updates add assets here without creating a new numbered release. Existing assets remain available for reproducible builds. Documentation update PR #8559 · Review the gallery Preview a bundle Download the archive selected by .github/actions/_lib/stage-browser-demos.sh , extract it, and enter its top-level directory. Then run: python -m http.server 8000 --directory site Open http://localhost:8000/interactive/ . The archive includes exporters/ , scene and rebuild instructions, licenses, and tools/publish.py . Running the demos needs only a browser. Rebuilding physics requires the pinned internal Newton Web compiler and Emscripten. Publish an update Reuse the interactive-releases publishing branch. Commit the reviewed site, create a commit-named archive and checksum, and upload both to this same release. Update the archive URL and SHA-256 together in the docs PR. Keep earlier assets and compatibility directories. The current publishing branch is available in the contributor fork . Creating it in the official repository requires an administrator under the repository's branch-creation rule. Runtime bundles are hosted in this official release and served by Isaac Lab documentation.

picked.title: MuJoCo 3.17.0
picked.summary: Version 3.17.0 (October 22, 2026) Significant new features c00ed8153 Added a batch API in mujoco/mjbatch.h (in Python as mujoco.batch ): many simulations of one model stepped on a thread pool of its own, each held as its integration state and loaded into an mjData for each call, so memory scales with threads and results are bit-identical to a plain loop at any thread count. It supports per-simulation model and option fields or models of the caller's, observations of the state after a step, recorded trajectories, persistent simulations (required for sleep), and arbitrary per-simulation functions. Follows the design of mjbatch by @kevinzakka . Engine Flex improvements: 94483e166 Added bending elasticity for 1D flexes, using a twist-free isotropic discrete elastic rod model. The cross-section is selected with the new section attribute: a circle of the flex radius, or a box with half-sizes sectionsize that uses the stiffness of its weak axis. It is enabled by a positive young modulus, requires a straight reference configuration (curved initial poses can be set with qpos or keyframes), is compatible with edge equality constraints, and is integrated implicitly by the discrete integrator. Previously young was ignored for 1D flexes: existing models that set it now bend, and fail to compile if the cross-section is degenerate (zero radius with the default circle section), if a vertex joins a zero-length edge, or if the rod is not straight. 36d0df9a5 , 897e3fcb1 Interpolated flexes ( trilinear or quadratic dofs ) now support self-collision , excluding elements in the same or neighboring cells. 39dd10f2d The default arena memory for flex models is now much smaller, sized from the flex mesh topology instead of nv^2 .
